   PLEASE SEND YOUR TEXTFILE!
Text is accepted in any form for
OUTLETTERS: wordprocessor files
(say which),typed or handwritten
letters. However, PLEASE send us
a textfile if possible so your
letter needn't be typed again!
The easiest for us to edit are
Tasword 2 files with the right
margin set at 32 but a textfile
in ANY format is appreciated!

Please state if there should be
parts of your letter you do not
wish published but we always use
our discretion anyway. Letters
may also be edited for clarity
and length... Please ask if you
welcome direct correspondence
from other OUTLET readers and we
will publish your full address.

From: John Couch

Dear Both,

I derive great enjoyment from
'Procross' and 'Prodata' but
have a slight problem with the
printout (Citizen 120D+). The
program gives me double-spacing
so the black squares don't link
up. I can, of course, cure the
problem by altering the dip-
switch configuration in the
interface. However, I then have
to alter it back for any other
program! Can I alter a line of
the BASIC to give me lesser
space between the lines?

Incidentally, how do I print the
pound sign? I get '.
                   - John Couch

Brian Cavers to John Couch

Use BREAK in PROCROSS to enter
BASIC.LIST 5300 and you will see
somewhere on the line...

LPRINT CHR$ 10;CHR$ 13

Delete the CHR$ 10 but leave the
CHR$ 13. The apostrophe (;) may
be left or not,it doesn't matter
in this position.

Do the same in line 5360.

Do the same in line 5390 but if
you look further along the line
there are four more CHR$ 10's.
These should be left alone -only
remove the single one earlier in
the line.

Finally, in line 5200 there are
a single CHR$ 10 AND one with a
CHR$ 13. BOTH the CHR$ 10's must
be removed and ALSO the LPRINT
with the single CHR$ 10.

I hope that wasn't too complex
to follow but write again if it
isn't clear. I have tested this
on my own printer with the dip
switch thrown and it does cure
the problem.

To print a "`" sign you need to
page in the English character
set on your printer and then
print CHR$ 35 (#). There are two
ways to do this. Your printer
should have a dipswitch that can
be altered (see your printer
manual). Then LPRINT "#".

However,you can't then LPRINT"#"
itself without sending an ESC
code first but you must choose
which you prefer as the default.

Once you have decided and set up
your dipswitch you need to send
the following codes to get the
other symbol...

    LPRINT CHR$ 27;"R";CHR$ 0

               ...and thereafter
LPRINT "#" will print a "#".

              or...

    LPRINT CHR$ 27;"R";CHR$ 3

               ...and thereafter
LPRINT "#" will print a "`".
                         - Brian

From John Hunter, OGMORE-BY-SEA



Dear Ron,

I have been trying to copy the
[FREEWARE] game SHANGHAI (OUTLET
46,SAM version) with,I'm afraid,
no luck.

I tried by LOADING the game then
breaking into BASIC then RS
RETURN (with a spare disk). All
that I got was the BASIC for the
game but none of the three code
routines (almost at the end of
OUTLET No.44). Being a very
"basic" enthusiast , I would
like to know if it is possible
to take a copy of SHANGHAI.

I also tried to COPY the program
BITCOPY in OUTLET No.43 with the
same disappointing results. That
program again I notice, has a
linking CODE section.

Incidentally, do you get many
readers corrupting their disks?
or am I unique! However if you
do - possibly a few words in
your editorial would help tyros
like myself.

        Yours sincerely,

          John Hunter

Brian Cavers to John Hunter

It would be nice if the RS way
would save all relevant code as
well as the BASIC but some code
is changed after loading and I
also use the RS myself over and
over again when editing the
BASIC and I don't like to keep
resaving the code as I might do
it once in a hundred times with
no code loaded (I would then
erase the original and lose the
lot!).

Therefore, the general rule for
saving OUTLET programs is enter
RS to save the BASIC.Try to load
the new copy. If it fails with a
"file not found" error then do
the following...

Note down the line number at the
end of the error report, e.g.,

107 file not found, 9000:2

 ...is statement 2 in line 9000.

LIST the line number.

Read through the line and note
down carefully the names of any
files that are loaded there.

Copy any such files using the
COPY command - or a program like
our CATLOADER (OUTLET 33). To
copy a file using COPY just put
the original disk in the drive
and COPY"NAME" TO "NAME".You can
also insert drive numbers if you
have two drives.

Spectrum owners can use similar
methods but instead of RS to
resave the BASIC use RUN 9972
for the +3, RUN 9982 for Opus,
Microdrive, Disciple/+D and RUN
9983 for tape. To copy code
files it's easiest to use our
CATLOADER (OUTLET 33 or the +D/
Disciple version in 44). Tape
users need a header reader like
CASSCAT (OUTLET 37) to find the
code details then load and save
them manually.

One of the most common reasons
for disc corruption on the SAM
is that when you press RESET it
often sends a current to the
drive causing it to corrupt any
disc therein. ALWAYS remove all
discs before a RESET.
                      - Brian

From:    Stuart Sumpter
        76 South Street,
    Stanground,Peterborough,

Dear Ron and Brian,

Congratulations on producing
such an excellent 'magazine'.
It's so refreshing to read a
magazine so "in tune" with its
readers. The only fault is its
size but the quality more than
compensates for that.

I have a Spectrum 48k+ and have
added on a Datel +D interface
and DSDD Drive.I would like to
do the following...

1) Connect my Spectrum to my
VCR and be able to record the
Spectrum's output.

2) To overlay graphics onto a
previously recorded film so, for
example, I can scroll a message
over the film..

I realise that this is a lot to
expect from my humble Speccy but
please leave my address at the
top of the letter so that kind
souls out there know where to
write if they have any inform-
ation such as other interfaces
and/or software.

Keep up the good work and all
the best for the future.
                    - S.Sumpter

Brian Cavers to S. Sumpter

We were all puzzled here as to
what you meant when you said,
"[OUTLET's] only fault is its
size..."! We were astonished
actually! We presume you meant
too small rather than too big
although we have had people
complain (lightheartedly)that it
contained TOO MUCH to digest in
one month!  You have the +D
version which has over 300K (and
often over 400K) of programs and
text! The SAM version has double
that(although this is mainly due
to the memory-hungry graphics).
Readers often ask how we cram in
so much. We use text and program
compression techniques. It is
hard to accept your "fault"!

I know of no video interface for
the Spectrum still commercially
available. If you can do some
simple soldering the following
works fine...

Get a video cable suitable for
the input on your video recorder
(consult your dealer). There are
two or three standard connectors
but you only need worry about
the end that plugs into your
video recorder.

If there is a plug on the other
end, cut it off and strip the
wire.

Open your Spectrum and you will
see a silver box in the top left
hand corner - the tv output.

You will see two wires connected
to the silver box on its left
side. Solder the outer shielding
wire of the cable to the silver
box connection which is nearest
the front of the Spectrum (as
you would normally use it). The
inner cable core wire should go
to the other connector.

You(and anyone else trying this)
will need to make provision for
anchoring the cable securely and
giving it exit from the Spectrum
but I leave this to individual
skill. You may need to drill the
case.

The foregoing also will give you
a better picture through your
video anyway.

I can take no responsibility for
damage to equipment! I can only
warn you to switch off and
disconnect everything, take care
when you detach and re-connect
the delicate keyboard membrane
and ALWAYS keep your fingers
crossed when you switch on again
else it won't work.

Overlaying Spectrum graphics on
video images is not practical (I
won't say impossible!) as there
is no hardware available to
synchronise the pictures and I'm
told it would be a horrendous
technical job to dabble in the
Spectrum's innards to find out
how! If you're determined to go
further then the Amiga is the
machine for advanced video work.
                        - Brian

Brian Cavers to Dominic Morris

Yes, any standard drive with a
standard Shugart connector will
connect to your +3 but you need
a special program to format the
disc. It just so happens that we
have just such a program in this
very issue! BFORMAT will format
your double-density,double-sided
drive to over 700K!Can't be bad.

It seems there is a flag byte at
the end (128, I think) which I
could not pin down. If I tried

something. Like you,I got newly-
declared variables "not found"!

However, I did find a method of
wrapping the whole lot of the
VARS area temporarily in a
string array and saving that and
it works fine. The program you
want is VARISAVE in OUTLET 26.It
is in regular use in PROCROSS to
save loads of different variable
data with each new crossword so
it is well-proven!

                         - Brian

From Bob Hobden, ROMFORD

Dear Ron and Brian,

First congratulations on an
excellent magazine.

I have started working my way
through OUTCLASS OUTLET EXTRA 1
and hope that you will consider
a future compilation disc of
OUTCLASS after issue 11.

Have you explained fully the use
of machine code REM statements?
If so, which issue? If not,could
you consider an article on the
subject?

Keep up the good work.

                   - Bob Hobden

Brian Cavers to Bob Hobden

Thanks, Bob. It is possible that
another compilation may be done
but there is nothing planned at
the moment. Incidentally, the
first few OUTCLASSes were ideal
for introducing the beginner.
Thereafter, BoB Smith has main-
tained a constant level of
moderate difficulty so one can
take any issue and learn a bit
from it. By that I mean,OUTCLASS
hasn't got harder and harder so
it's impossible to follow. Once
anyone has grasped the first
introductory issues and the main
principles it's then a matter of
learning a little more from any
issue. BoB Smith is also always
willing to answer queries.

Next month we have a program to
put code into REM statements the
easy way. However, here is what
is actually happening...

The BASIC listing you see is a
sequence of values in memory
that the BASIC interpreter in
the Spectrum or SAM interprets
as line numbers or keywords etc.
When you LIST, the computer
looks through memory where the
BASIC program is and displays
the right character, keyword or
number according to the values
in memory. For example, if the
Spectrum finds an address with
252 in then it prints the word
DRAW because the value 252
represents the keyword DRAW on
the Spectrum.

The computer then looks at the
next address. If it's say,65, it
will put an "A" next to the word
DRAW (65 represents capital A).

You can POKE different values in
the memory occupied by the BASIC
program just as you can POKE any
area of RAM memory but if you
POKE a wrong value in the wrong
place BASIC goes wrong! Memory
used by text in a REM statement
is safe because when you RUN a
program,BASIC ignores the memory
just after a REM and jumps ahead
to the memory further on where
the next BASIC line starts. If
you had a REM followed by 10 x's
then the 10 x's are in memory
and may be POKED with say 10 b's
or you can POKE any 10 values
from 0 to 255.

The trick is to find the right
addresses in memory to POKE! If
you add, remove or alter any of
the lines before the REM line
then the computer moves ALL the
following BASIC lines, including
the REM line, in memory to make
room or close up the gap so the
REM is not even at a fixed place
in memory!

There are several methods of
finding the address of a REM. If
you put the REM in the first
line (line 1) then you can work
out the position from the system
variable which has the address
of the start of BASIC. However,
many values upset the printing
of the LIST so I prefer to put
such REMs near the end of BASIC.

To achieve this,I use the system
variable that has the address of
the "next line of BASIC". This
system variable is at addresses
23637 and 23638 on the Spectrum
and 23196, 23197 and 23198 on
the SAM. If you think about it,
the address of the start of the
next line is also one more than
the LAST address of the current
line so if you put a PEEK of the
system variable in say, line 50
and if you know the length of
line 50 then you can calculate
backwards the address of the
start of line 50. There is no
actual system variable to point
at the current line while the
program is running(but there are
other methods of finding it,e.g,
the DATA address sysvar).

On the Spectrum, if you enter...

50 LET NX=PEEK 23637 + 256* PEEK
   23638:REM xxxxxxxxxx

60 PRINT NX

            ...then line 60 will
print the address of the start
of line 60. The value 13 is put
at the end of every BASIC line
so if you subtract ONE from NX
you will have the address of the
13 at the end of line 50 (the 13
is not visible in the listing,it
only causes the LIST to start a
new line). If you then subtract
another ONE you will have the
address of the LAST x in line 50
and subtracting another 9 gets
you the address of the first x.

Altogether then, you need to
subtract 11 from NX to find the
start of the x's so if you add..

70 FOR A=NX-11 TO NX-2
80 PRINT CHR$ PEEK A;
90 NEXT A

               ...you should get
10 x's printed on the screen.

Incidentally, SAM owners should
substitute this line 50...

  50 LET NX=(PEEK 23196-1)*16384
     + PEEK 23197+256*PEEK 23198
     : REM xxxxxxxxxx

(the third address has the page
of RAM in which the address is
placed).

If you substitute...

80 POKE A,CODE "b"

    ...in the above then the x's
will be replaced by b's. In the
same way you can POKE machine
code, character sets, UDGS, even
SCREEN$ etc.

I'll leave it to you to study
the REMs at the end of nearly
all OUTLET programs to see how
the foregoing is condensed into
one line and includes a USR call
to run a machine code routine in
the REM memory.

                        - Brian

From: Gordon Roberts, CUMBRIA

Dear Outleteers,

      Rubbish from Roberts

1. Better TV picture? Try using
the lead which connects a video
recorder to a TV. i.e. Plug the
TV lead from your computer into
the appropriate end of the video
lead and connect the other end
of the video lead to your TV.
This does give a better picture.
I suspect it works rather like
Brian Gaff's Atari 800XL lead.
On a colour TV, take off some of
the colour - adjust to taste.

2. Write programs on a +3 using
Beta Basic 3.0!"How?",I hear you
all shout.

Coming soon in OUTLET is my pro-
gram which allows this.You must,
of course. have the original
copy of BB3.0 from which you can
extract the CODE and "LINE 0".

3. "Legible" tip. When editing
in 128 mode have BRIGHT set to
"1" then, when you enter "PRINT
A$ or w.h.y? or "LIST", you will
be able to see what is displayed
without having to clear the
screen to avoid it being mixed
up amongst your program listing.

4. You must have heard of EOF.
How about EOcatalogue?On the +3,
SAVE a file as CHR$(127), the
copyright symbol,and it will
always be the LAST in a cat
(unless you have one saved as
CHR$(127)ALICE, of course).

5. You all know the +3 does not
particularly like you attempting
to edit program lines that are
too long. Well, when editing a
long line, keep it in the middle
of the screen (room at the top
and room at the bottom), then,
when you press ENTER, the cursor
will not "go walkabout".

Has anyone had problems trying
to edit CATLOADER [+3 VERSION].
For example, the computer
locking up in an irrecoverable
machine code loop or going into
a BASIC loop which prints the
page and clears the screen and
round and round it goes or
sometimes there is a parameter
error working on files on page
2?

Also, after copying files and
then pressing EDIT for a cat
there is a stop with a NONSENSE
IN BASIC error. A program of my
own does this too. I suspect it
might be something to do with
the RAM PAGING? To avoid this
happening DON'T do a cat right
after copying; use one of the
other options first.

That's all for now.

EXCEPT - Let's hear it for Brian
and Ron for a job brilliantly
carried out. Hip, Hip, Hoorah!
Please keep up the good work.

               Bye,

         Gordon Roberts

P.S. I have just taken delivery
of a sheet feeder for my
Mannesmann Tally MT81 printer.
CONTINUOUS (fanfold) paper has
now become OBSOLETE so far as I
am concerned. The system now
"grabs" a sheet as it needs one,
prints it and then "spits it
out" and so on. Wonderful! No
hassle with perforations any
more.


Thanks,Gordon. Editing ANY BASIC
in 128K mode may result in a
crash if there is code in REMs
I've found. It's the same on the
SAM. The other oddities are also
+3 buglets I think.

                        - Brian.

From Ken Hunter, NORTH YORKS.



Dear Ron,

When we were speaking on the
phone the other day about some-
thing else I mentioned that I
had a little amendment to my
DZINER program (OUTLET 41) which
would enable Plus D users with
an Epson FX80 compatible printer
to print their works of art
after they had created them on
the screen and here it is...

All that is needed is to break
into BASIC with DZINER running
and then to type in and enter
these two lines...

 490 IF CODE INKEY$ = 4 THEN
     GOSUB 1350:SAVE SCREEN$ 1:
     GOSUB 1220


 492 IF CODE INKEY$ = 5 THEN
     GOSUB 1350:SAVE SCREEN$ 2:
     GOSUB 1220



With these two lines in,pressing
TRUE VIDEO will produce a screen
dump of the picture 32 cols wide
or pressing INV VIDEO will give
a large-size screendump 10
inches wide, printed lengthwise
down the paper and with tones of
grey for the colours.

I haven't had an opportunity yet
to experiment with the "POKE@"
routines which you suggested to
cure the double line spaces that
I get when printing text from
OUTLET but I shall soon and I
thank you very much for your
help with this little problem.

        All good wishes,

           Ken Hunter





Many thanks, Ken

                - Brian Cavers

From: Les Harding, DARTFORD

Dear Ron & Brian,

I was wondering if there is
someone who knows a way of
producing the large 'HEADLINER'
fonts in P.C.G's Wordmaster
D.T.P. program for the Speccy.

I've tried to contact P.C.G.
using their answerphone but as
yet have had no reply. So, if
anyone could give me a few
pointers as to how to tackle
this problem I would be most
grateful!

While I'm on the subject of
'WORDMASTER' (which I think is a
superb program), perhaps I could

suggest, if there is room in
'OUTLET', that we could have a
'hints and tips' section for
those who use it and maybe even
swap files that readers have
produced that they think may be
useful for other users. What do
you think, Ron?

Anyway, to start the ball
rolling I've a little 'tip' for
'WORDMASTER' users which might
seem obvious to some but I
thought it worth a mention
anyhow especially for those
using microdrives.

With only approx. 85K of storage
on the average microdrive cart-
ridge SAVing several screen$ of
graphics which need, on average,

about 7K for each one, can soon
gobble up valuable space. This
became quite apparent when
trying to SAVE the CLIP ART on
OUTLET for future use in
'WORDMASTER'.

I'd noticed, as no doubt so has
anyone who uses this program,
that when screen$ are LOADed in
they occupy much less space than
they did when residing on the
cartridge. Obviously they are
being compressed automatically.
After a little experimenting I
found that in most cases I could
at least double the amount of
screen$ I could store on a
single cartridge and sometimes a
bit more,depending on the nature
of the screen$.

The procedure is as follows:
Firstly LOAD the graphic screen$
as normal using the 'graph' key.
It's preferable to LOAD as many
screen$ as possible with which
the memory can cope.This saves a
bit of time for the next stage.

Secondly, 'GET' the graphic file
of your choice. You will then be
presented with a menu of
options. One of these is to SAVE
the file either with its present
name or as something else.

Thirdly after SAVing you will be
returned to the main menu screen
showing the graphic you have
just dealt with complete with
its current name at the bottom
of the list.

Repeat this procedure until you
have dealt with all the graphic
files.


If you now do a catalogue (K) of
the cartridge you can see how
much room you have left. I think
you will be quite surprised!.


To LOAD the newly-SAVEd
compressed files back into
'WORDMASTER' for future use you
do NOT use the 'graph' key as
before but instead the (L)oad
key as you would for a text
file. If you do try to LOAD it
using the 'graph' key, you will
just get a load of meaningless
blobs on the screen.

So much for the good news!!...
Now the drawbacks! (As they say,
'You get now't for now't in this
world'.)

The only minor iritation I have
found with this method is that
the graphics cannot be LOADed
again as normal screen$ hence it
will not be possible to LOAD
them back into an art package to
do any alterations so make sure
you get them right first!

Now come on you lot out there,
let's get those ideas rolling
in!

          All the best

               Les

Brian Cavers to Les Harding

A hints and tips section which
specializes in one subject would
have to develop naturally by the
amount of material contributed.
For now, anyone is welcome to
send in ideas on DTP and tips,
etc. These will go in OUTLETTERS
while longer articles will go in
DRIVECHAT or OUTPUT. The best
thing anyone interested can do
is to send in something on the
subject. Items from half a dozen
different people will almost
certainly draw response from
even more readers as we have
witnessed on other subjects. If
anyone would like to do a series
of articles however,let me know!

                       - Brian

Dear Brian,

I have not seen any comments on
Jon North's brilliant "HOW 2
HACK" series [YOUR SINCLAIR] in

Brian Cavers to Bob Hobden

Thanks, Bob. It is possible that another compilation may be done but there is nothing planned at the moment. Incidentally, the first few OUTCLASSes were ideal for introducing the beginner. Thereafter, BoB Smith has main- tained a constant level of moderate difficulty so one can take any issue and learn a bit from it. By that I mean,OUTCLASS hasn't got harder and harder so it's impossible to follow. Once anyone has grasped the first introductory issues and the main principles it's then a matter of learning a little more from any issue. BoB Smith is also always willing to answer queries.

Next month we have a program to put code into REM statements the easy way. However, here is what is actually happening...

The BASIC listing you see is a sequence of values in memory that the BASIC interpreter in the Spectrum or SAM interprets as line numbers or keywords etc. When you LIST, the computer looks through memory where the BASIC program is and displays the right character, keyword or number according to the values in memory. For example, if the Spectrum finds an address with 252 in then it prints the word DRAW because the value 252 represents the keyword DRAW on the Spectrum.

The computer then looks at the next address. If it's say,65, it will put an "A" next to the word DRAW (65 represents capital A).

You can POKE different values in the memory occupied by the BASIC program just as you can POKE any area of RAM memory but if you POKE a wrong value in the wrong place BASIC goes wrong! Memory used by text in a REM statement is safe because when you RUN a program,BASIC ignores the memory just after a REM and jumps ahead to the memory further on where the next BASIC line starts. If you had a REM followed by 10 x's then the 10 x's are in memory and may be POKED with say 10 b's or you can POKE any 10 values from 0 to 255.

The trick is to find the right addresses in memory to POKE! If you add, remove or alter any of the lines before the REM line then the computer moves ALL the following BASIC lines, including the REM line, in memory to make room or close up the gap so the REM is not even at a fixed place in memory!

There are several methods of finding the address of a REM. If you put the REM in the first line (line 1) then you can work out the position from the system variable which has the address of the start of BASIC. However, many values upset the printing of the LIST so I prefer to put such REMs near the end of BASIC.

To achieve this,I use the system variable that has the address of the "next line of BASIC". This system variable is at addresses 23637 and 23638 on the Spectrum and 23196, 23197 and 23198 on the SAM. If you think about it, the address of the start of the next line is also one more than the LAST address of the current line so if you put a PEEK of the system variable in say, line 50 and if you know the length of line 50 then you can calculate backwards the address of the start of line 50. There is no actual system variable to point at the current line while the program is running(but there are other methods of finding it,e.g, the DATA address sysvar).

On the Spectrum, if you enter...

50 LET NX=PEEK 23637 + 256* PEEK 23638:REM xxxxxxxxxx

60 PRINT NX

...then line 60 will print the address of the start of line 60. The value 13 is put at the end of every BASIC line so if you subtract ONE from NX you will have the address of the 13 at the end of line 50 (the 13 is not visible in the listing,it only causes the LIST to start a new line). If you then subtract another ONE you will have the address of the LAST x in line 50 and subtracting another 9 gets you the address of the first x.

Altogether then, you need to subtract 11 from NX to find the start of the x's so if you add..

70 FOR A=NX-11 TO NX-2 80 PRINT CHR$ PEEK A; 90 NEXT A

...you should get 10 x's printed on the screen.

Incidentally, SAM owners should substitute this line 50...

50 LET NX=(PEEK 23196-1)*16384 + PEEK 23197+256*PEEK 23198 : REM xxxxxxxxxx

(the third address has the page of RAM in which the address is placed).

If you substitute...

80 POKE A,CODE "b"

...in the above then the x's will be replaced by b's. In the same way you can POKE machine code, character sets, UDGS, even SCREEN$ etc.

I'll leave it to you to study the REMs at the end of nearly all OUTLET programs to see how the foregoing is condensed into one line and includes a USR call to run a machine code routine in the REM memory.

Anyway, to start the ball rolling I've a little 'tip' for 'WORDMASTER' users which might seem obvious to some but I thought it worth a mention anyhow especially for those using microdrives.

With only approx. 85K of storage on the average microdrive cart- ridge SAVing several screen$ of graphics which need, on average,

about 7K for each one, can soon gobble up valuable space. This became quite apparent when trying to SAVE the CLIP ART on OUTLET for future use in 'WORDMASTER'.

I'd noticed, as no doubt so has anyone who uses this program, that when screen$ are LOADed in they occupy much less space than they did when residing on the cartridge. Obviously they are being compressed automatically. After a little experimenting I found that in most cases I could at least double the amount of screen$ I could store on a single cartridge and sometimes a bit more,depending on the nature of the screen$.

The procedure is as follows: Firstly LOAD the graphic screen$ as normal using the 'graph' key. It's preferable to LOAD as many screen$ as possible with which the memory can cope.This saves a bit of time for the next stage.

Secondly, 'GET' the graphic file of your choice. You will then be presented with a menu of options. One of these is to SAVE the file either with its present name or as something else.

Thirdly after SAVing you will be returned to the main menu screen showing the graphic you have just dealt with complete with its current name at the bottom of the list.

Repeat this procedure until you have dealt with all the graphic files.

If you now do a catalogue (K) of the cartridge you can see how much room you have left. I think you will be quite surprised!.

To LOAD the newly-SAVEd compressed files back into 'WORDMASTER' for future use you do NOT use the 'graph' key as before but instead the (L)oad key as you would for a text file. If you do try to LOAD it using the 'graph' key, you will just get a load of meaningless blobs on the screen.

So much for the good news!!... Now the drawbacks! (As they say, 'You get now't for now't in this world'.)

The only minor iritation I have found with this method is that the graphics cannot be LOADed again as normal screen$ hence it will not be possible to LOAD them back into an art package to do any alterations so make sure you get them right first!

LPRINT CHR$ 10;CHR$ 13

```text
LPRINT CHR$ 27;"R";CHR$ 0
```

...и после этого `LPRINT "#"` напечатает «#».

или...

```text
LPRINT CHR$ 27;"R";CHR$ 3
```

...и после этого `LPRINT "#"` напечатает «£».

В следующем месяце у нас будет программа для легкого помещения кода в операторы REM. Однако вот что на самом деле происходит «под капотом»...

Листинг на BASIC, который вы видите — это последовательность значений в памяти, которую интерпретатор BASIC в Спектруме или SAM воспринимает как номера строк, ключевые слова и т. д. При выполнении команды LIST компьютер просматривает память, где находится программа на BASIC, и выводит нужный символ, ключевое слово или число в соответствии со значениями в памяти. Например, если Спектрум находит адрес со значением 252, он печатает слово DRAW, потому что значение 252 представляет токен DRAW на Спектруме.

Затем компьютер смотрит следующий адрес. Если там, скажем, 65, он выведет «A» сразу за словом DRAW (65 представляет заглавную букву A).

Вы можете заносить разные значения по POKE в память, занятую программой на BASIC, точно так же, как и в любую другую область RAM, но если занести неправильное значение в неподходящее место, BASIC просто сломается! Память, используемая текстом в операторе REM, безопасна, потому что при запуске программы (RUN) BASIC игнорирует память сразу за REM и перескакивает вперед к тому месту, где начинается следующая строка BASIC. Если у вас был REM, за которым следовали 10 символов «x», то эти 10 «x» лежат в памяти, и их можно заменить через POKE, например, на 10 символов «b» или любые 10 значений от 0 до 255.

Фокус в том, чтобы найти правильные адреса в памяти для POKE! Если вы добавите, удалите или измените любую строку перед строкой с REM, компьютер сдвинет ВСЕ последующие строки BASIC (включая строку REM) в памяти, чтобы освободить место или убрать пустоту, так что REM даже не находится на фиксированном месте!

Есть несколько способов найти адрес REM. Если поместить REM в самую первую строку (строка 1), то позицию можно вычислить по системной переменной, содержащей адрес начала BASIC. Однако многие значения портят печать при выводе листинга по LIST, поэтому я предпочитаю размещать такие REM ближе к концу BASIC-программы.

Для этого я использую системную переменную, хранящую адрес «следующей строки BASIC». Эта системная переменная находится по адресам 23637 и 23638 на Спектруме и 23196, 23197 и 23198 на SAM. Если подумать, адрес начала следующей строки также ровно на единицу больше, чем ПОСЛЕДНИЙ адрес текущей строки. Поэтому, если считать системную переменную через PEEK, скажем, в строке 50, и если вы знаете длину строки 50, то можно отсчитать назад адрес начала строки 50. Системной переменной, указывающей непосредственно на текущую выполняемую строку, в системе нет (хотя есть другие способы ее найти, например, через системную переменную адреса данных DATA).

На Спектруме, если вы введете:

```text
50 LET NX=PEEK 23637 + 256* PEEK 23638:REM xxxxxxxxxx
60 PRINT NX
```

...то строка 60 напечатает адрес начала строки 60. Значение 13 помещается в конце каждой строки BASIC, поэтому, если отнять ЕДИНИЦУ от NX, вы получите адрес того самого кода 13 в конце строки 50 (байт 13 не виден в листинге, он лишь заставляет команду LIST начать новую строку). Если затем отнять еще ЕДИНИЦУ, вы получите адрес ПОСЛЕДНЕГО «x» в строке 50, а вычитание еще 9 даст адрес первого «x».

Таким образом, чтобы найти начало символов «x», нужно вычесть 11 из NX. Поэтому, если добавить:

```text
70 FOR A=NX-11 TO NX-2
80 PRINT CHR$ PEEK A;
90 NEXT A
```

...на экране должно напечататься 10 символов «x».

К слову, владельцам SAM следует заменить строку 50 на такую:

```text
50 LET NX=(PEEK 23196-1)*16384 + PEEK 23197+256*PEEK 23198 : REM xxxxxxxxxx
```

(третий адрес содержит страницу RAM, в которой находится этот адрес).

Если вы замените:

```text
80 POKE A,CODE "b"
```

...в примере выше, то «x» заменятся на «b». Таким же образом вы можете заносить по POKE машинный код, наборы символов, графику пользователя (UDG), даже целый SCREEN$ и т. д.

Я предоставлю вам самим изучить строки REM в конце почти всех программ OUTLET, чтобы увидеть, как всё вышеописанное сжимается в одну строку и включает вызов USR для запуска процедуры в машинном коде прямо из памяти REM.

В любом случае, чтобы положить начало, у меня есть маленький «секрет» для пользователей 'WORDMASTER'. Кому-то он покажется очевидным, но я счел нужным упомянуть о нем, особенно для тех, кто пользуется микродрайвами.

При среднем объеме картриджа микродрайва всего около 85K, сохранение (SAVE) нескольких графических экранов screen$, каждый из которых «весит» в среднем около 7K, может быстро сожрать драгоценное место. Это стало совершенно очевидно при попытке сохранить CLIP ART из OUTLET для дальнейшего использования в 'WORDMASTER'.

Я заметил (как, без сомнения, и все, кто работает с этой программой), что когда экраны screen$ загружаются (LOAD), они занимают гораздо меньше места, чем на картридже. Очевидно, они автоматически сжимаются. Проведя пару экспериментов, я обнаружил, что в большинстве случаев можно как минимум удвоить количество экранов, помещающихся на один картридж, а иногда и больше — в зависимости от характера самого экрана screen$.

Порядок действий следующий:
Во-первых, загрузите (LOAD) графический screen$ как обычно, используя клавишу 'graph'. Предпочтительно загрузить столько экранов, сколько позволит память. Это сэкономит время на следующем этапе.

Во-вторых, выберите нужный графический файл командой 'GET'. Перед вами появится меню опций. Одна из них — сохранить (SAVE) файл либо под его текущим именем, либо под другим.

В-третьих, после сохранения вы вернетесь в главное меню экрана, где будет показана только что обработанная графика с ее текущим именем внизу списка.

Повторяйте эту процедуру, пока не обработаете все графические файлы.

Если вы теперь выполните каталог (K) картриджа, то сможете увидеть, сколько места у вас осталось. Думаю, вы будете весьма удивлены!

Чтобы ЗАГРУЗИТЬ (LOAD) только что СОХРАНЕННЫЕ (SAVEd) сжатые файлы обратно в 'WORDMASTER' для дальнейшего использования, вы НЕ используете клавишу 'graph', как раньше, а вместо этого используете клавишу (L)oad, как если бы вы загружали обычный текстовый файл. Если вы попытаетесь ЗАГРУЗИТЬ их с помощью клавиши 'graph', вы получите лишь кучу бессмысленных пятен на экране.

А теперь давайте, ребята, присылайте свои идеи!

Всего наилучшего,
